title: Ulyana and the Harvest
premise: Mirabel Ashgrove, a pest controller who has spent two decades rationalizing the inexplicable, is summoned to her late grandmother's farmhouse where every photograph now contains an extra empty chair — and the chair moves closer in each one. She discovers the house keeps a 'count': every generation it harvests one family member, and this year the count falls due on the autumn equinox. As Mirabel digs into her grandmother's ledgers and learns the family's prosperity was bought with these sacrifices, she must decide whether to pay the debt, break it, or pass it on. In the end, Mirabel burns the ledger and offers herself in place of her niece — but the house, cheated of its chosen heir, takes the inheritance itself, collapsing into the earth with the harvest uncollected, leaving the family free but forever listening for noises.
about_author: Kestrel Lockridge is the pen name of a former rural insurance adjuster who spent years documenting claims no actuary could explain. They write horror from a farmhouse in upstate New York, where they keep the photographs face-down at night.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A routine call about scratching in the walls of her grandmother's vacant farmhouse turns strange when Mirabel notices an unfamiliar wooden chair in every family photograph — including ones taken decades apart. The emotional beat is dread disguised as professional calm; her rationalizations begin to crack.

chapters.title: Scratching Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Still Mirabel's POV. Investigating the crawlspace, she finds claw-marks that match no animal she knows, arranged in tally marks. Her radio picks up a child counting backward from one hundred. The beat: the pest controller realizes she may be the infestation's next target.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledgers
chapters.summary: Mirabel finds a locked writing desk containing ledgers dating to 1898, each autumn marked with a name struck through and the word 'PAID.' The final page lists her own name, undated. Beat: cold recognition that the family has always known.

chapters.title: The Family Gathers
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Mirabel's brother Dale, arriving with his wife and daughter Wren for the estate reading. He mocks Mirabel's warnings; the house feels warm and welcoming to them. Beat: dramatic irony — the reader sees the trap closing while the family relaxes into it.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Want
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Overnight, the extra chair in the photos has moved from the parlor corner to the head of the dinner table. Wren, sleepwalking, sets a fifth plate for breakfast. Beat: escalating wrongness; Mirabel stops explaining and starts believing.

chapters.title: Aunt Hettie Remembers
chapters.summary: POV of elderly Aunt Hettie, driven from a care home by dreams of the house. She tells Mirabel of 1974, when her sister 'went to live with grandma' and was never spoken of again. Beat: grief and complicity — the survivors chose not to look.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Mirabel deciphers the ledger: the house takes one Ashgrove each generation, always near the equinox, always the one who inherits. The deed names Wren as sole beneficiary. Beat: horror sharpened into urgency — nine days remain.

chapters.title: Dale Signs the Papers
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. A charming lawyer arrives to expedite probate; Dale signs, eager for money, dismissing Mirabel's objections as grief-fueled mania. That night he dreams of sitting in the extra chair. Beat: corruption begins; the house rewards cooperation.

chapters.title: Wren's Invisible Friend
chapters.summary: POV alternates between Wren and Mirabel. Wren describes playing with 'the tall lady' who asks her questions about being tired. Mirabel finds chalk handprints on Wren's ceiling. Beat: maternal terror; the stakes become a child.

chapters.title: Burning the Ledger
chapters.summary: Mirabel burns the ledgers in the woodstove. The fire goes green, then out; the ashes reassemble themselves on the hearth, pages blank except her name, now dated: the equinox. Beat: false victory curdling into despair — the house cannot be argued with.

chapters.title: The Neighbors Know
chapters.summary: Mirabel visits neighboring farms. Every property within sight of the Ashgrove land has flourished; every family has a missing member and a locked room. An old farmer tells her: 'We don't ask what the ground eats.' Beat: the horror is communal, sanctioned, ancient.

chapters.title: Hettie's Confession
chapters.summary: Hettie reveals she was meant to be taken in 1974 but pushed her sister forward instead. The house accepted the substitution once. She believes it can be tricked again — or bargained with. Beat: hope with a rotten core; survival built on betrayal.

chapters.title: Dale Locks the Doors
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. The house begins rewarding him — promotions, luck, money appearing in accounts — if he keeps the family inside. He changes the locks and hides the car keys. Beat: power corrupting in real time; brother against sister.

chapters.title: The Tall Lady
chapters.summary: Mirabel confronts the entity directly in the parlor at 3 a.m.: a figure like her grandmother, stretched wrong, seated in the extra chair. It speaks only in questions about who is tired, who is ready to rest. Beat: confrontation without resolution; terror made intimate.

chapters.title: Running
chapters.summary: Mirabel attempts to flee with Wren at dawn. The road loops back to the farmhouse no matter which direction they drive. Wren, oddly calm, says the tall lady told her the count must be met before anyone leaves. Beat: claustrophobic futility; escape is impossible.

chapters.title: The Substitution
chapters.summary: Hettie proposes repeating 1974: offer someone willing, someone old, someone guilty. She volunteers herself. Mirabel refuses to let another woman be sacrificed for the family's comfort. Beat: moral crisis — is breaking the cycle worth defying the only person offering a way out?

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The house prepares itself: doors opening onto hallways that shouldn't exist, the dinner table set for five, the extra chair drawn close to Wren's place. Dale, half-besotted by the house's gifts, welcomes it. Beat: dread at full pressure; the family gathers for their own harvest.

chapters.title: The Dinner
chapters.summary: Climax begins. At dinner, the tall lady presides. Dale, entranced, tries to seat Wren in the chair; Mirabel fights him as the walls fill with the faces of all the harvested Ashgroves. Beat: chaos, betrayal, and love colliding at the table.

chapters.title: What Mirabel Offers
chapters.summary: Climax. Mirabel claims the inheritance herself, signing the deed over to her own name, and sits in the chair — offering twenty years of guilt and a life spent explaining away the noises. The house hesitates, hungry for a child but bound by the count's rules. Beat: sacrifice as both surrender and defiance.

chapters.title: The House Refuses
chapters.summary: Climax resolves. The house, cheated of its chosen heir, tries to take everything; Mirabel, inside the chair's grip, recites the names from the ledger aloud, returning every debt at once. The foundation splits, the tall lady unravels into ash, and the house folds inward. Beat: cathartic destruction at terrible cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, weeks later. She survived, pulled from the rubble with the ledger fused to her hands. The family scatters; Dale won't speak to her; Wren sleeps soundly for the first time. But the lot where the house stood is greener than anywhere for miles. Beat: exhausted relief shadowed by unease.

chapters.title: Listening
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Mirabel's POV. In her city apartment, Mirabel unpacks the salvaged photographs. In every one, the extra chair is gone — but in the newest photo, taken last week, there is a faint scratching sound when she looks at it too long. She does not explain it. Beat: quiet, unresolved dread; some counts are never closed.
